content:
Numbers 16 shows us that rebellion against Yahweh did not end in one single judgment. Different groups were judged in different ways, and each judgment matched the seriousness of their rebellion. As we look at the chapter today, we will see three distinct judgments fall, one after another, each one revealing how seriously God regarded the sin of rising up against the order He had established.

First came the judgment upon Korah, Dathan, and Abiram. Moses had warned the congregation to move away from their tents and not even to touch anything that belonged to them. Then, as soon as Moses finished speaking, the ground split open. The Scripture says, "The earth opened its mouth and swallowed them up" (Numbers 16:32). Dathan and Abiram, their households, and those associated with the rebellion went down alive into the pit, and the earth closed over them. Later, Numbers 26:10 summarizes this judgment by connecting Korah with Dathan and Abiram in the same rebellion. This was not an ordinary death. Yahweh Himself gave an unmistakable sign that these men had despised His order and rejected the servants He had appointed. The very ground beneath their feet became the instrument of their judgment, so that all Israel would know beyond any doubt that these men had set themselves against Yahweh.

Then came the judgment upon the two hundred and fifty leaders who had joined Korah. These men had taken censers and offered incense before Yahweh, even though that priestly service had never been given to them. Their rebellion was therefore not only against Moses and Aaron, but against the order Yahweh had established. The Scripture says, "A fire came out from Yahweh and consumed the two hundred and fifty men who were offering incense" (Numbers 16:35). Notice how fitting this judgment was. The very act by which they tried to claim priestly privilege became the place of their judgment. They lifted up censers to seize an honour Yahweh had not given them, and from those very censers the fire of judgment met them. Yahweh showed clearly that no one could simply take holy service upon himself because he desired it.

What is not given by Yahweh cannot be seized by man.

After witnessing these two fearful judgments, one would surely expect the congregation to fear God and repent. But the very next day, the people gathered again against Moses and Aaron and said, "You have killed the people of Yahweh" (Numbers 16:41). They had seen the earth open. They had seen fire come out from Yahweh. And yet they still blamed Moses and Aaron, and even called the rebels who had been judged "the people of Yahweh." Because the congregation hardened their hearts once more, Yahweh sent a plague among them, and it spread quickly through the camp. Moses immediately understood the danger and told Aaron to take his censer, put in fire and incense, and make atonement for the people. Aaron did not stand at a safe distance. He ran into the very middle of the congregation and stood between the living and the dead. The Scripture says, "He stood between the dead and the living; so, the plague was stopped" (Numbers 16:48). But before the plague was stopped, fourteen thousand seven hundred people had died, besides those who had died in Korah's rebellion (Numbers 16:49).

So, the judgments in Numbers 16 were clear and severe. The earth swallowed the rebels. Fire consumed the two hundred and fifty leaders. A plague struck the congregation, and fourteen thousand seven hundred died. These judgments reveal how seriously Yahweh regarded rebellion, jealousy, false accusation, and the refusal to repent even after the clearest correction. And yet, even in the middle of such terrible judgment, we see a picture of mercy, for Aaron the priest ran into the midst of the dying and made atonement, and the plague was stopped. The very priesthood that Korah had despised became the means by which the remaining people were spared. Judgment and mercy stood side by side in that camp, the fire of God on one hand, and a priest standing between the dead and the living on the other.

This is a fearful chapter, because the people did not simply make one mistake. Rebellion continued even after God had judged it openly, again and again.

And the warning it gives us is very clear: when Yahweh corrects, the right response is humility and repentance, not another accusation. Israel answered every correction with a fresh complaint, and each fresh complaint brought a fresh judgment. But the way of life is the opposite. When God rebukes us,we are to bow low, confess our sin, and return quickly to obedience.The Scripture says, "He who is often rebuked, and hardens his neck, will suddenly be destroyed, and that without remedy" (Proverbs 29:1). May the New Creation never harden the heart after correction, but quickly return to obedience under Christ Jesus, who is our great High Priest, standing between us and the judgment we deserve. Tomorrow, God willing, we will study more of this chapter and the lessons it holds for us.

title: Prayer
text:
Our Father, whose judgments are righteous and whose mercy is great,
We have seen how seriously You regard rebellion against the order You establish.

Teach us that what You have not given, we must never try to seize for ourselves.

When You correct us, keep us from answering with a fresh complaint or accusation.

Make us quick to bow low, confess our sin, and return at once to obedience.

We thank You for our great High Priest, who stands between us and the judgment we deserve.

"He who conceals his sins does not prosper, but whoever confesses and renounces them finds mercy." - Proverbs 28:13

In Christ’s name, our High Priest, we pray. Amen.
